newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian navy heads to yachtsmen's rescue.
newsitem.headline: Australian navy heads to yachtsmen's rescue.

text.p: Australian rescuers held out hope on Wednesday for the survival of a British solo yachtsman as a navy frigate steamed towards the Antarctic where a second solo sailor waits to be plucked from a life raft.

Rescuers believe Tony Bullimore, 56, may be inside the hull of his upturned yacht, Global Exide Challenger, although listening devices dropped into the sea on Wednesday failed to pick up any signs of life.
"We are disappointed we haven't heard anything, but we are very hopeful we will hear," Australian Defence Force spokesman Colonel Andrew Reynolds told Reuters.
"It does not mean because we have not heard...that he is not there or that he is dead."

Bullimore and 29-year-old Thierry Dubois, competitors in the Vendee Globe round-the-world race, capsized in wild seas on Sunday after hitting a storm about 900 miles from Antarctica and 1,400 miles from the Australian coast.
Dubois was found by a rescue plane a day later clinging to the upturned hull of his yacht Pour Amnesty International and managed to scramble aboard a life raft dropped from the air.
Bullimore has not been sighted but hopes for his safety were raised on Tuesday when one of his two distress beacons was switched to alert status, an operation that can only be done manually.

The captain of the Royal Australian Navy frigate heading to the region said a bid to lift Dubois from his raft by helicopter late on Wednesday had been postponed due to low cloud and freezing conditions which made it unsafe to fly.

HMAS Adelaide's Captain Raydon Gates told Reuters that a helicopter rescue would be attempted at first light on Thursday, although weather conditions had deteriorated, with 50 knot winds and five metre (16 ft) high waves.
If conditions were unsafe for the helicopter, a boat would be launched later from the the frigate to try to reach Dubois.
"He is dry, which is very important," Gates said. "His spirits are down a bit obviously as the nights crawl on but he is aware that we are going to pick him up tomorrow morning."
HMAS Adelaide would then head 60 miles south to Bullimore's yacht, but could spend only 12 hours in the search zone.
Gates said the yacht's manufacturers had told the navy that Bullimore could survive reasonably well in the yacht's two living spaces and would have about 140 hours of air.
"If he's in his anti-immersion suit and he is out of the water in that upturned yacht he has a reasonable chance of still being alive when I reach him," he said.
Rescuers would try to establish contact with Bullimore through the hull so he could swim out, or would attempt to cut a hole into the yacht, he said.

The two yachtsmen were the latest competitors in the Vendee Globe round-the-world race to hit disaster in the stormy seas south of Australia. Frenchman Rafael Dinelli, 28, arrived in Hobart, Tasmania, earlier on Wednesday after he was rescued from a life raft by a fellow competitor two days after Christmas.
